claim: ZNF165 is a CT antigen frequently expressed in triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC).
source: Here we report that ZNF165, a CT antigen frequently expressed in triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC), associates with SMAD3 to modulate transcription of transforming growth factor β (TGFβ)-dependent genes and thereby promote growth and survival of human TNBC cells.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a characterization of ZNF165.

claim: ZNF165 associates with SMAD3 to modulate transcription of TGFβ-dependent genes.
source: Here we report that ZNF165, a CT antigen frequently expressed in triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC), associates with SMAD3 to modulate transcription of transforming growth factor β (TGFβ)-dependent genes and thereby promote growth and survival of human TNBC cells.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: ZNF165 promotes growth and survival of human TNBC cells.
source: Here we report that ZNF165, a CT antigen frequently expressed in triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC), associates with SMAD3 to modulate transcription of transforming growth factor β (TGFβ)-dependent genes and thereby promote growth and survival of human TNBC cells.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data.

claim: ZNF446 is an obligate component of the ZNF165-SMAD3 complex.
source: In addition, we identify the KRAB zinc finger protein, ZNF446, and its associated tripartite motif protein, TRIM27, as obligate components of the ZNF165-SMAD3 complex that also support tumor cell viability.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data.

claim: TRIM27 is an obligate component of the ZNF165-SMAD3 complex.
source: In addition, we identify the KRAB zinc finger protein, ZNF446, and its associated tripartite motif protein, TRIM27, as obligate components of the ZNF165-SMAD3 complex that also support tumor cell viability.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data.

claim: ZNF446 and TRIM27 support tumor cell viability.
source: In addition, we identify the KRAB zinc finger protein, ZNF446, and its associated tripartite motif protein, TRIM27, as obligate components of the ZNF165-SMAD3 complex that also support tumor cell viability.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data.

claim: TRIM27 is necessary for ZNF165 transcriptional activity.
source: Importantly, we find that TRIM27 alone is necessary for ZNF165 transcriptional activity and is required for TNBC tumor growth in vivo using an orthotopic xenograft model in immunocompromised mice.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data.

claim: TRIM27 is required for TNBC tumor growth in vivo using an orthotopic xenograft model in immunocompromised mice.
source: Importantly, we find that TRIM27 alone is necessary for ZNF165 transcriptional activity and is required for TNBC tumor growth in vivo using an orthotopic xenograft model in immunocompromised mice.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data from xenograft studies.

claim: Aberrant expression of a testis-specific transcription factor is sufficient to co-opt somatic transcriptional machinery to drive a pro-tumorigenic gene expression program in TNBC.
source: Our findings indicate that aberrant expression of a testis-specific transcription factor is sufficient to co-opt somatic transcriptional machinery to drive a pro-tumorigenic gene expression program in TNBC.
evidence: This is the main conclusion stated in the abstract, based on the experimental findings.

claim: There are approximately 270 cancer/testis (CT) genes.
source: Given this feature, these ~270 genes are collectively termed cancer/testis (CT) genes and their encoded proteins are known as CT antigens (Simpson et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to support the number.

claim: CT antigens have long been considered attractive targets for immunotherapy in a wide variety of cancers.
source: CT antigens have long been considered attractive targets for immunotherapy in a wide variety of cancers (Whitehurst, 2014; Thomas et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to support the claim.

claim: Many CT antigens can support neoplastic behaviors in tumor cells.
source: In addition, recent work from multiple groups has found that many CT antigens can support neoplastic behaviors in tumor cells (Gibbs and Whitehurst, 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to support the claim.

claim: CT antigens have been implicated in supporting mitotic progression, degradation of tumor suppressors, promoting DNA repair and thwarting apoptosis.
source: Specifically, CT antigens have been implicated in supporting mitotic progression, degradation of tumor suppressors, promoting DNA repair and thwarting apoptosis (Whitehurst et al., 2010; Hosoya et al., 2011; Cappell et al., 2012; Maxfield et al., 2015; Pineda et al., 2015; Viphakone et al., 2015; Nichols et al., 2018; Gallegos et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with multiple citations to support the claim.

claim: ZNF165 was previously identified as essential for triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) survival.
source: Using a large-scale, loss-of-function screening approach, our group previously identified the CT antigen, ZNF165, as essential for triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) survival (Maxfield et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to previous work.

claim: Depletion of ZNF165 in vitro or in vivo reduces survival of TNBC cells.
source: Depletion of ZNF165 in vitro or in vivo reduces survival of TNBC cells.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with reference to previous work.

claim: Elevated ZNF165 mRNA expression correlates significantly with reduced survival time in breast cancer.
source: Importantly, elevated ZNF165 mRNA expression correlates significantly with reduced survival time in breast cancer, indicating that expression of this protein may confer an aggressive tumorigenic phenotype (Maxfield et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to previous work.

claim: ZNF165 is a C2H2 zinc finger transcription factor that contains an N-terminal SCAN domain and six canonical Zn2+ fingers at its C-terminus.
source: ZNF165 is a C2H2 zinc finger transcription factor that contains an N-terminal SCAN domain and six canonical Zn2+ fingers at its C-terminus.
evidence: This is a structural description of ZNF165 stated in the introduction.

claim: ZNF165 expression is restricted to human testes and is extremely low or undetectable in normal breast tissues.
source: Consistent with its characterization as a CT antigen, ZNF165 expression is restricted to human testes and is extremely low or undetectable in normal breast tissues (Tirosvoutis et al., 1995; Maxfield et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to support the claim.

claim: ZNF165 lacks conservation in mice.
source: Unfortunately, ZNF165 lacks conservation in mice, thereby precluding genetic studies that could illuminate its normal function within the testes (Tirosvoutis et al., 1995).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to support the claim.

claim: ZNF165 associates with chromatin to regulate expression of its target genes.
source: However, investigation of its function in TNBC revealed that ZNF165 associates with chromatin to regulate expression of its target genes, which includes approximately 25% of all TGFβ-responsive genes in TNBC cells (Maxfield et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to previous work.

claim: ZNF165 regulates approximately 25% of all TGFβ-responsive genes in TNBC cells.
source: However, investigation of its function in TNBC revealed that ZNF165 associates with chromatin to regulate expression of its target genes, which includes approximately 25% of all TGFβ-responsive genes in TNBC cells (Maxfield et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to previous work.

claim: TGFβ is well known to facilitate growth inhibition in breast epithelia and most other somatic tissues.
source: For example, TGFβ is well known to facilitate growth inhibition in breast epithelia and most other somatic tissues, primarily through transcriptional activation of cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitors that result in cell cycle arrest (Hannon and Beach, 1994; Polyak et al., 1994; Morikawa et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to support the claim.

claim: TGFβ has been shown to stimulate the growth and differentiation of multiple cell types, including chondrocytes, hematopoietic stem cells, and endothelial cells.
source: Conversely, TGFβ has also been shown to stimulate the growth and differentiation of multiple cell types, including chondrocytes, hematopoietic stem cells, and endothelial cells (Goumans et al., 2002; Li et al., 2005; Challen et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to support the claim.

claim: Contrasting responses to TGFβ are generally dictated by cell type-specific transcription factors, which associate with TGFβ-responsive SMAD proteins (SMAD3 and SMAD4).
source: These contrasting responses to TGFβ are generally dictated by cell type-specific transcription factors, which associate with TGFβ-responsive SMAD proteins (SMAD3 and SMAD4) and recruit them to appropriate target genes for transcriptional regulation (Chen et al., 2002; Gomis et al., 2006; Mullen et al., 2011; Massagué, 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to support the claim.

claim: In TNBC, TGFβ induces a metastatic phenotype by promoting survival, chemoresistance, and the epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition.
source: In TNBC, TGFβ induces a metastatic phenotype by promoting survival, chemoresistance, and the epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (Massagué, 2008; Bhola et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to support the claim.

claim: SMAD3 expression is elevated in late-stage breast tumors compared to other receptor-activated SMADs.
source: Notably, SMAD3 expression is elevated in late-stage breast tumors compared to other receptor-activated SMADs (Tian et al., 2003; Padua et al., 2008; Petersen et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to support the claim.

claim: SMAD3 binding is associated with over 27,000 sites in WHIM12 cells.
source: We found that SMAD3 binding is associated with over >27,000 sites in WHIM12 cells, comparable to previous studies of SMAD3 binding in TNBC cell lines (Tufegdzic Vidakovic et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a finding from the ChIP-seq experiments reported in the Results section.

claim: Over 90% of ZNF165 target genes are also bound by SMAD3.
source: Intersecting SMAD3 and ZNF165-associated genes revealed that >90% of ZNF165 target genes are also bound by SMAD3, an overlap representing a statistically significant enrichment (p=5.5e-120, hypergeometric distribution) (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is a finding from the ChIP-seq analysis reported in the Results section and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: 90% of shared ZNF165-SMAD3 targets were bound by both transcription factors at a distance of less than 100 kb from one another.
source: Mapping the distance between binding sites further revealed that 90% of shared targets were bound by both transcription factors at a distance of less than 100 kb from one another (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is a finding from the ChIP-seq analysis reported in the Results section and shown in Figure 1B.

claim: 36% of shared target genes had ZNF165 and SMAD3 binding sites within 1 kb.
source: Furthermore, 36% of shared target genes had ZNF165 and SMAD3 binding sites within 1 kb, a proximity at which both factors exhibited overlap on chromatin due to the broad enrichment profile of SMAD3 as observed within our dataset (Figure 1B–E).
evidence: This is a finding from the ChIP-seq analysis reported in the Results section and shown in Figure 1B-E.

claim: WHIM12 cells were originally developed from a patient-derived xenograft established from a triple-negative, highly chemo-resistant tumor.
source: WHIM12 cells were originally developed from a patient-derived xenograft established from a triple-negative, highly chemo-resistant tumor (Li et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with a citation.

claim: WHIM12 cells are classified within the claudin-low molecular subtype of breast cancer, which exhibits activated TGFβ signaling.
source: Moreover, these cells are classified within the claudin-low molecular subtype of breast cancer, which exhibits activated TGFβ signaling (Prat et al., 2010; Asiedu et al., 2011; Sabatier et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citations.

claim: 118 sites were identified where ZNF165 and SMAD3 were bound within 1 kb of each other in WHIM12 cells.
source: We identified 118 sites where ZNF165 and SMAD3 were bound within 1 kb of each other in WHIM12 cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the ChIP-seq analysis reported in the Results section.

claim: More than 50% of ZNF165-SMAD3 co-bound sites were present in gene promoters.
source: More than 50% of these ZNF165-SMAD3 co-bound sites were present in gene promoters (−1 kb or +100 base pairs from TSS) while the majority of SMAD3 binding sites were generally distributed across different genomic regions (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is a finding from the ChIP-seq analysis reported in the Results section and shown in Figure 1F.

claim: GC-rich motifs are significantly present at the ZNF165-SMAD3 co-bound regions compared to those bound by ZNF165 alone.
source: Motif enrichment analysis revealed a significant presence of GC-rich motifs at the ZNF165-SMAD3 co-bound regions (n = 118) compared to those bound by ZNF165 alone (n = 204) (Figure 1G and H).
evidence: This is a finding from the motif enrichment analysis reported in the Results section and shown in Figure 1G and H.

claim: GC-rich SMAD binding elements (SBEs) have been characterized as universal binding sites for receptor-activated SMAD proteins.
source: Such GC-rich SMAD binding elements (SBEs) have recently been characterized as universal binding sites for receptor-activated SMAD proteins, and SMAD3 can bind variants of these motifs with high affinity (Martin-Malpartida et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with a citation.

claim: Elevated ZNF165 expression in patients with breast cancer is associated with a greater metastatic potential (Hazard Ratio (HR) = 1.4; p=0.004).
source: Consistent with this, elevated ZNF165 expression in patients with breast cancer is associated with a greater metastatic potential (Hazard Ratio (HR) = 1.4; p=0.004) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: This is a finding from survival analysis reported in the Results section and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1H.

claim: There is a significant correlation (r = 0.52) between expression fold-changes in response to depletion of ZNF165 or SMAD3.
source: This analysis revealed a significant correlation (r = 0.52) between expression fold-changes in response to depletion of either transcription factor (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is a finding from gene expression analysis reported in the Results section and shown in Figure 2A.

claim: ZNF165 and SMAD3 were required to either activate or repress expression of the majority of shared target genes.
source: In particular, ZNF165 and SMAD3 were required to either activate or repress expression of the majority of shared target genes (quadrant I and III, Figure 2A).
evidence: This is a finding from gene expression analysis reported in the Results section and shown in Figure 2A.

claim: ZNF165 knockdown resulted in a ~50% reduction of SMAD3 enrichment at the ZNF165 binding sites proximal to both SMURF2 and RRAD.
source: ZNF165 knockdown resulted in a ~ 50% reduction of SMAD3 enrichment at the ZNF165 binding sites proximal to both SMURF2 and RRAD (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is a finding from ChIP-qPCR experiments reported in the Results section and shown in Figure 2D.

claim: SMAD3 binding at the promoter of LBH, a site not co-bound by ZNF165, was unaffected by ZNF165 depletion.
source: Importantly, SMAD3 binding at the promoter of LBH, a site not co-bound by ZNF165, was unaffected by ZNF165 depletion.
evidence: This is a finding from ChIP-qPCR experiments reported in the Results section.

claim: A reduction of H3K27ac at the ZNF165-SMAD3 binding site proximal to RRAD was observed in response to ZNF165 knockdown.
source: Consistent with this, we observed a reduction of H3K27ac at the ZNF165-SMAD3 binding site proximal to RRAD in response to ZNF165 knockdown (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is a finding from ChIP-qPCR experiments reported in the Results section and shown in Figure 2E.

claim: An increase in H3K27ac was detected upon ZNF165 overexpression.
source: Conversely, an increase in H3K27ac was detected upon ZNF165 overexpression (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is a finding from ChIP-qPCR experiments reported in the Results section and shown in Figure 2F.

claim: SMURF2 is a well characterized negative regulator of the TGFβ pathway whose expression is activated in a TGFβ-dependent, SMAD-independent manner by PI3K signaling.
source: Indeed, SMURF2 is a well characterized negative regulator of the TGFβ pathway whose expression is activated in a TGFβ-dependent, SMAD-independent manner by PI3K signaling (Ohashi et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with a citation.

claim: RRAD is sufficient to promote proliferation of breast tumor cells in vitro and in vivo.
source: In addition, a report from 2001 indicated that RRAD is sufficient to promote proliferation of breast tumor cells in vitro and in vivo (Tseng et al., 2001).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with a citation.

claim: In the mesenchymal subtype of TNBC, RRAD expression correlated with reduced overall survival (HR = 2.31; p=0.04).
source: In the mesenchymal subtype of TNBC, which is enriched for active TGFβ signaling and an EMT gene expression signature, RRAD expression correlated with reduced overall survival (HR = 2.31; p=0.04) and greater metastatic potential (HR = 3.18; p=0.05) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B; Lehmann et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a finding from survival analysis reported in the Results section and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: In the mesenchymal subtype of TNBC, RRAD expression correlated with greater metastatic potential (HR = 3.18; p=0.05).
source: In the mesenchymal subtype of TNBC, which is enriched for active TGFβ signaling and an EMT gene expression signature, RRAD expression correlated with reduced overall survival (HR = 2.31; p=0.04) and greater metastatic potential (HR = 3.18; p=0.05) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B; Lehmann et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a finding from survival analysis reported in the Results section and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: In luminal tumors, RRAD expression correlated with improved overall survival (HR = 0.63; p=0.01).
source: Conversely, in luminal tumors, which are traditionally ER+ and exhibit tumor-suppressive TGFβ signaling, RRAD expression correlated with improved overall survival (HR = 0.63; p=0.01) and no correlation was observed with distant metastasis free survival (HR = 1.12; p=0.55) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C; Perou et al., 2000; Sato et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a finding from survival analysis reported in the Results section and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: In luminal tumors, no correlation was observed between RRAD expression and distant metastasis free survival (HR = 1.12; p=0.55).
source: Conversely, in luminal tumors, which are traditionally ER+ and exhibit tumor-suppressive TGFβ signaling, RRAD expression correlated with improved overall survival (HR = 0.63; p=0.01) and no correlation was observed with distant metastasis free survival (HR = 1.12; p=0.55) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C; Perou et al., 2000; Sato et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a finding from survival analysis reported in the Results section and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: RRAD was essential for growth of SUM159 cells in soft agar.
source: Moreover, DepMap analysis revealed that RRAD perturbation generally leads to a reduction in 2D growth of TNBC cell lines, and we found that RRAD was essential for growth of SUM159 cells in soft agar (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D and E).
evidence: This is a finding from soft agar assays reported in the Results section and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1E.

claim: ZNF165 and SMAD3 physically associate.
source: Interaction studies using co-expression/co-immunoprecipitation indicated an association between ZNF165 and SMAD3 (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a finding from co-immunoprecipitation experiments reported in the Results section and shown in Figure 3A.

claim: ZNF165 interacts with the active, phosphorylated form of SMAD3 on chromatin in SUM159 cells.
source: In addition, we found that ZNF165 interacts with the active, phosphorylated form of SMAD3 on chromatin in SUM159 cells stably expressing ZNF165-V5 (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is a finding from ChIP experiments reported in the Results section and shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The endogenous association between ZNF165 and SMAD3 is significantly diminished by pre-treatment with SB-431542.
source: Proximity ligation assays (PLAs) in SUM159 cells treated with TGFβ revealed an endogenous association between ZNF165 and SMAD3, which was significantly diminished by pre-treatment with SB-431542 (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is a finding from proximity ligation assays reported in the Results section and shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Endogenous ZNF165 and SMAD4 interact in a TGFβ-dependent manner.
source: Furthermore, we found that endogenous ZNF165 and SMAD4 also interact in a TGFβ-dependent manner (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is a finding from proximity ligation assays reported in the Results section and shown in Figure 3E.

claim: ChIP-seq analysis did not reveal the presence of ZNF165 binding sites near the SMAD3 or SMAD4 gene loci.
source: Importantly, ChIP-seq analysis did not reveal the presence of ZNF165 binding sites near the SMAD3 or SMAD4 gene loci (Maxfield et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with a citation to previous work.

claim: 48 putative ZNF165 interacting partners were identified from yeast two-hybrid screening.
source: This search returned 48 putative ZNF165 interacting partners, 17 of which are likely transcriptional regulators based on the presence of known gene regulatory domains (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is a finding from yeast two-hybrid screening reported in the Results section.

claim: 17 of the 48 putative ZNF165 interacting partners are likely transcriptional regulators based on the presence of known gene regulatory domains.
source: This search returned 48 putative ZNF165 interacting partners, 17 of which are likely transcriptional regulators based on the presence of known gene regulatory domains (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is a finding from analysis of yeast two-hybrid screening data reported in the Results section.

claim: Five putative ZNF165 interactors with SCAN domains were identified.
source: We identified five putative interactors with SCAN domains and examined the consequences of their depletion on SMURF2 expression.
evidence: This is a finding from analysis of yeast two-hybrid screening data reported in the Results section.

claim: ZNF446 and SCAND1 phenocopied the changes in gene expression observed for ZNF165 and SMAD3 in two TNBC cell lines.
source: Of the proteins tested, ZNF446 and SCAND1 phenocopied the changes in gene expression observed for ZNF165 and SMAD3 in two TNBC cell lines (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is a finding from gene expression analysis reported in the Results section and shown in Figure 4B.

claim: ZNF446 is upregulated in breast tumors.
source: Examination of their tumor expression patterns revealed that ZNF446 is upregulated in breast tumors, an increase that trends with reduced survival in the triple-negative enriched basal-like subtype of breast cancer (HR = 1.89; p=0.059) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and B; Perou et al., 2000; Sørlie et al., 2001).
evidence: This is a finding from tumor expression analysis reported in the Results section and shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: ZNF446 upregulation trends with reduced survival in the triple-negative enriched basal-like subtype of breast cancer (HR = 1.89; p=0.059).
source: Examination of their tumor expression patterns revealed that ZNF446 is upregulated in breast tumors, an increase that trends with reduced survival in the triple-negative enriched basal-like subtype of breast cancer (HR = 1.89; p=0.059) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and B; Perou et al., 2000; Sørlie et al., 2001).
evidence: This is a finding from survival analysis reported in the Results section and shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Depletion of ZNF446 significantly reduced anchorage-independent growth of TNBC cells.
source: Moreover, we found that depletion of ZNF446 significantly reduced anchorage-independent growth of TNBC cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is a finding from soft agar assays reported in the Results section and shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: ZNF165 and ZNF446 interact.
source: Co-expression/co-immunoprecipitation assays confirmed that ZNF165 and ZNF446 interact and that deletion of the ZNF165 SCAN domain abrogates this association (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is a finding from co-immunoprecipitation experiments reported in the Results section and shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Deletion of the ZNF165 SCAN domain abrogates the association between ZNF165 and ZNF446.
source: Co-expression/co-immunoprecipitation assays confirmed that ZNF165 and ZNF446 interact and that deletion of the ZNF165 SCAN domain abrogates this association (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is a finding from co-immunoprecipitation experiments reported in the Results section and shown in Figure 4C.

claim: An endogenous interaction between ZNF165 and ZNF446 is detectable in TNBC tumor cell nuclear extracts.
source: In addition, an endogenous interaction between ZNF165 and ZNF446 was detectable in TNBC tumor cell nuclear extracts, confirming these proteins interact in the relevant subcellular compartment (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is a finding from immunoprecipitation experiments reported in the Results section and shown in Figure 4D.

claim: ZNF446 interacts with both SMAD3 and SMAD4 in a TGFβ-dependent fashion.
source: We then employed the SMAD3/4 PLA assay described above and found that ZNF446 interacts with both SMAD3 and SMAD4 in a TGFβ-dependent fashion, similar to ZNF165 (Figure 4E and F).
evidence: This is a finding from proximity ligation assays reported in the Results section and shown in Figure 4E and F.

claim: 5039 ZNF446 binding sites were identified in WHIM12 cells.
source: This led to the identification of 5039 and 7926 binding sites in WHIM12 and SUM159 cells, respectively.
evidence: This is a finding from ChIP-seq experiments reported in the Results section.

claim: 7926 ZNF446 binding sites were identified in SUM159 cells.
source: This led to the identification of 5039 and 7926 binding sites in WHIM12 and SUM159 cells, respectively.
evidence: This is a finding from ChIP-seq experiments reported in the Results section.

claim: In both WHIM12 and SUM159 cell lines, ZNF446 was enriched at the ZNF165 binding sites.
source: In both cell lines, ZNF446 was enriched at the ZNF165 binding sites (Figure 5A and B; Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: This is a finding from ChIP-seq analysis reported in the Results section and shown in Figure 5A and B.

claim: There is a statistically significant overlap between ZNF446 and ZNF165 target genes in both WHIM12 and SUM159 cells (p<0.0001).
source: Intersecting the target genes identified for ZNF446 and ZNF165 further revealed a statistically significant overlap in both WHIM12 and SUM159 cells (p<0.0001, hypergeometric distribution) (Figure 5C and D).
evidence: This is a finding from ChIP-seq analysis reported in the Results section and shown in Figure 5C and D.

claim: Approximately half of all ZNF446 binding sites in WHIM12 cells were also co-occupied by SMAD3.
source: Approximately half of all ZNF446 binding sites in WHIM12 cells were also co-occupied by SMAD3 (Figure 5E and F; Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is a finding from ChIP-seq analysis reported in the Results section and shown in Figure 5E and F.

claim: ZNF446-SMAD3 co-bound sites were largely enriched for promoter regions compared to the total binding sites for either factor.
source: These co-bound sites were largely enriched for promoter regions compared to the total binding sites for either factor (Figure 5—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is a finding from ChIP-seq analysis reported in the Results section and shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1E.

claim: A short GC-rich element is present at ZNF446-SMAD3 bound sites, closely resembling the motif identified at ZNF165-SMAD3 bound sites.
source: Differential motif enrichment analysis revealed the presence of a short GC-rich element at these ZNF446-SMAD3 bound sites, closely resembling the motif we identified at ZNF165-SMAD3 bound sites and identical to the recently reported SMAD consensus binding motif (Figure 5G and H; Figure 1G; Martin-Malpartida et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a finding from motif enrichment analysis reported in the Results section and shown in Figure 5G and H.

claim: Over half of the TGFβ-responsive target genes shared by ZNF165 and SMAD3 (251/446) are also targeted by ZNF446.
source: In addition, we found that over half of the TGFβ-responsive target genes shared by ZNF165 and SMAD3 (251/446) are also targeted by ZNF446 (Figure 5I).
evidence: This is a finding from ChIP-seq analysis reported in the Results section and shown in Figure 5I.

claim: The impact of ZNF446 depletion on expression of shared target genes significantly correlated with both ZNF165 (r = 0.49) and SMAD3 (r = 0.86).
source: The impact of ZNF446 depletion on expression of these genes significantly correlated with both ZNF165 (r = 0.49) and SMAD3 (r = 0.86) (Figure 5J).
evidence: This is a finding from gene expression analysis reported in the Results section and shown in Figure 5J.

claim: ZNF446 contains a KRAB domain.
source: ZNF446 contains a KRAB (Krüppel-associated box) domain, which is well documented to interact with the RBCC (RING, B-box, coiled-coil) domain of proteins within the tripartite motif (TRIM) family that in turn function as co-repressors or, as recently demonstrated, co-activators (Friedman et al., 1996; Schultz et al., 2001; Schultz et al., 2002; Chen et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citations.

claim: KRAB domains interact with the RBCC domain of proteins within the tripartite motif (TRIM) family.
source: ZNF446 contains a KRAB (Krüppel-associated box) domain, which is well documented to interact with the RBCC (RING, B-box, coiled-coil) domain of proteins within the tripartite motif (TRIM) family that in turn function as co-repressors or, as recently demonstrated, co-activators (Friedman et al., 1996; Schultz et al., 2001; Schultz et al., 2002; Chen et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citations.

claim: Y2H-based proteomics confirmed an interaction between TRIM27 and ZNF446.
source: Y2H-based proteomics confirmed such an interaction of TRIM27, which contains the classic RBCC domain, with ZNF446 (Figure 6A; Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is a finding from yeast two-hybrid screening reported in the Results section.

claim: TRIM27 was originally identified as an oncogenic fusion with the RET tyrosine kinase.
source: Originally identified as an oncogenic fusion with the RET tyrosine kinase, TRIM27 has been ascribed roles in numerous cellular processes that include transcriptional repression, proliferation, meiosis, innate immunity, and endosomal trafficking (Takahashi et al., 1985; Shimono et al., 2000; Shimono et al., 2003; Zha et al., 2006; Hao et al., 2013; Zaman et al., 2013; Zheng et al., 2015; Ma et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citations.

claim: TRIM27 has been ascribed roles in transcriptional repression, proliferation, meiosis, innate immunity, and endosomal trafficking.
source: Originally identified as an oncogenic fusion with the RET tyrosine kinase, TRIM27 has been ascribed roles in numerous cellular processes that include transcriptional repression, proliferation, meiosis, innate immunity, and endosomal trafficking (Takahashi et al., 1985; Shimono et al., 2000; Shimono et al., 2003; Zha et al., 2006; Hao et al., 2013; Zaman et al., 2013; Zheng et al., 2015; Ma et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citations.

claim: Both ZNF446 and ZNF165 interact with TRIM27.
source: Co-expression/co-immunoprecipitation experiments revealed that both ZNF446 and ZNF165 interact with TRIM27 and that all three proteins immunoprecipitate as a complex (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is a finding from co-immunoprecipitation experiments reported in the Results section and shown in Figure 6B.

claim: ZNF165, ZNF446, and TRIM27 immunoprecipitate as a complex.
source: Co-expression/co-immunoprecipitation experiments revealed that both ZNF446 and ZNF165 interact with TRIM27 and that all three proteins immunoprecipitate as a complex (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is a finding from co-immunoprecipitation experiments reported in the Results section and shown in Figure 6B.

claim: A nuclear interaction between ZNF165-V5 and endogenous TRIM27 was confirmed by proximity ligation in SUM159 cells.
source: We subsequently confirmed a nuclear interaction between ZNF165-V5 and endogenous TRIM27 by proximity ligation in SUM159 cells and found that TRIM27 depletion also phenocopied changes in ZNF165-SMAD3 target gene expression (r = 0.81) (Figure 6C and D).
evidence: This is a finding from proximity ligation assays reported in the Results section and shown in Figure 6C.

claim: TRIM27 depletion phenocopied changes in ZNF165-SMAD3 target gene expression (r = 0.81).
source: We subsequently confirmed a nuclear interaction between ZNF165-V5 and endogenous TRIM27 by proximity ligation in SUM159 cells and found that TRIM27 depletion also phenocopied changes in ZNF165-SMAD3 target gene expression (r = 0.81) (Figure 6C and D).
evidence: This is a finding from gene expression analysis reported in the Results section and shown in Figure 6D.

claim: TRIM27 is required for the transcriptional activation of RRAD following ZNF165 or ZNF446 overexpression.
source: Indicative of a co-activator function, we found that TRIM27 is required for the transcriptional activation of RRAD following ZNF165 or ZNF446 overexpression (Figure 6E; Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a finding from gene expression analysis reported in the Results section and shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Proximity ligation assays revealed endogenous, nuclear interactions between TRIM27 and both SMAD3 and SMAD4, which were reduced by TGFβ pathway inhibition.
source: Similar to ZNF165 and ZNF446, proximity ligation assays revealed endogenous, nuclear interactions between TRIM27 and both SMAD3 and SMAD4, which were reduced by TGFβ pathway inhibition (Figure 6F and G).
evidence: This is a finding from proximity ligation assays reported in the Results section and shown in Figure 6F and G.

claim: TRIM27 expression is elevated in several cancers including colon, lung, endometrial and ovarian, and often correlates with poor prognosis.
source: TRIM27 expression is elevated in several cancers including colon, lung, endometrial and ovarian, and often correlates with poor prognosis (Tsukamoto et al., 2009; Horio et al., 2012; Iwakoshi et al., 2012; Zoumpoulidou et al., 2012; Ma et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citations.

claim: TRIM27 expression is significantly elevated in TNBC compared to normal breast tissue.
source: Using TCGA data, we found that TRIM27 expression is significantly elevated in TNBC compared to normal breast tissue (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is a finding from TCGA data analysis reported in the Results section and shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: TRIM27 appeared to be predominantly cytoplasmic in normal breast epithelia and more nuclear in TNBC tissues.
source: Moreover, we stained a small cohort of normal and TNBC tissues for TRIM27 and observed a striking difference in its subcellular localization. TRIM27 appeared to be predominantly cytoplasmic in normal breast epithelia and more nuclear in TNBC tissues, suggesting that its transcriptional activity might associate with the transformed state (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is a finding from immunohistochemistry reported in the Results section and shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1C.

claim: TRIM27 is mostly cytoplasmic in normal breast and nuclear in testis and a subset of breast cancer tissues.
source: This finding is in agreement with previous reports and the Human Tissue Atlas, where TRIM27 is mostly cytoplasmic in normal breast and nuclear in testis and a subset of breast cancer tissues (Tezel et al., 1999; Tezel et al., 2009; Uhlén et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citations.

claim: TRIM27 depletion dramatically reduced tumor cell growth in the absence of extracellular matrix.
source: In the absence of extracellular matrix, TRIM27 depletion dramatically reduced tumor cell growth (Figure 6—figure supplement 1D–F).
evidence: This is a finding from soft agar assays reported in the Results section and shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1D-F.

claim: TRIM27 depletion resulted in a significant decrease in tumor size in an orthotopic xenograft model.
source: We observed a significant decrease in tumor size, suggesting that TRIM27 is essential for TNBC tumor growth in vivo and that inhibition of the ZNF165 transcriptional complex may be a promising avenue of therapeutic intervention (Figure 6H and I).
evidence: This is a finding from orthotopic xenograft experiments reported in the Results section and shown in Figure 6H and I.

claim: TRIM27 is essential for TNBC tumor growth in vivo.
source: We observed a significant decrease in tumor size, suggesting that TRIM27 is essential for TNBC tumor growth in vivo and that inhibition of the ZNF165 transcriptional complex may be a promising avenue of therapeutic intervention (Figure 6H and I).
evidence: This is a conclusion from orthotopic xenograft experiments reported in the Results section and shown in Figure 6H and I.

claim: Inhibition of the ZNF165 transcriptional complex may be a promising avenue of therapeutic intervention.
source: We observed a significant decrease in tumor size, suggesting that TRIM27 is essential for TNBC tumor growth in vivo and that inhibition of the ZNF165 transcriptional complex may be a promising avenue of therapeutic intervention (Figure 6H and I).
evidence: This is a conclusion from orthotopic xenograft experiments reported in the Results section.

claim: TRIM27 is a previously unrecognized regulatory component of TGFβ signaling in TNBC.
source: Together, these results indicate that TRIM27 is a previously unrecognized regulatory component of TGFβ signaling in TNBC and functions to modulate TGFβ-dependent transcription in cooperation with ZNF165, ZNF446, and SMAD3.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Results section based on the experimental findings.

claim: TRIM27 functions to modulate TGFβ-dependent transcription in cooperation with ZNF165, ZNF446, and SMAD3.
source: Together, these results indicate that TRIM27 is a previously unrecognized regulatory component of TGFβ signaling in TNBC and functions to modulate TGFβ-dependent transcription in cooperation with ZNF165, ZNF446, and SMAD3.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Results section based on the experimental findings.

claim: Striking similarities between tumors and developing germ cells have been noted for over a century.
source: Striking similarities between tumors and developing germ cells have been noted for over a century (Simpson et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with a citation.

claim: A fundamental attribute of cancer is the usurpation of developmental signaling programs.
source: As a result, it has been speculated that a fundamental attribute of cancer is the usurpation of developmental signaling programs.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a speculation.

claim: The vast majority of zinc finger proteins contain KRAB, BTB/POZ, or SCAN domains.
source: The vast majority of these proteins contain KRAB, BTB/POZ, or SCAN domains, that mediate interactions with transcriptional partners (Bellefroid et al., 1991; Bardwell and Treisman, 1994; Albagli et al., 1995; Williams et al., 1995).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citations.

claim: The SCAN domain regulates the assembly and thus function of specific transcriptional complexes.
source: The SCAN domain in particular regulates the assembly and thus function of specific transcriptional complexes (Edelstein and Collins, 2005).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with a citation.

claim: SCAN domains demonstrate selectivity for co-association.
source: SCAN domains are not promiscuous, but demonstrate selectivity for co-association, the basis of which is not clear.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section.

claim: Ectopic introduction of a SCAN domain-containing protein, such as ZNF165, may drive assembly of a neomorphic transcriptional complex.
source: Nevertheless, ectopic introduction of a SCAN domain-containing protein, such as ZNF165, may drive assembly of a neomorphic transcriptional complex, ZNF165-ZNF446-SMAD3-TRIM27, that is otherwise not present in somatic cells (Figure 7).
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Discussion section based on the experimental findings.

claim: ZNF446 has been reported to act as a transcriptional repressor for SRF and AP-1 via its KRAB domain.
source: While ZNF446 has been reported to act as a transcriptional repressor for SRF and AP-1 via its KRAB domain, a physiological function for ZNF446 in either normal or malignant contexts has not been reported (Liu et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with a citation.

claim: A physiological function for ZNF446 in either normal or malignant contexts has not been reported.
source: While ZNF446 has been reported to act as a transcriptional repressor for SRF and AP-1 via its KRAB domain, a physiological function for ZNF446 in either normal or malignant contexts has not been reported (Liu et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with a citation.

claim: ZNF446 may recruit TRIM27 to modulate TGFβ-induced transcription in TNBC.
source: Our findings suggest that in addition to functioning as a chromatin-bound cofactor for ZNF165 and SMAD3, ZNF446 may recruit TRIM27 to modulate TGFβ-induced transcription in TNBC.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Discussion section based on the experimental findings.

claim: ZNF446 and TRIM27 can either activate or repress expression of genes targeted by the ZNF165-SMAD3 complex.
source: Regardless, we find that ZNF446 and TRIM27 can either activate or repress expression of genes targeted by the ZNF165-SMAD3 complex, despite reports describing only repressive capabilities for these factors (Shimono et al., 2000; Shimono et al., 2003; Liu et al., 2005).
evidence: This is a finding stated in the Discussion section.

claim: TRIM28 serves as a co-activator for ZFP30-mediated adipogenesis.
source: This finding also dovetails with a recent report demonstrating that TRIM28 serves as a co-activator for ZFP30-mediated adipogenesis, and together these studies begin to establish that tripartite motif proteins may be bi-functional with respect to transcriptional repression or activation (Chen et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with a citation.

claim: Tripartite motif proteins may be bi-functional with respect to transcriptional repression or activation.
source: This finding also dovetails with a recent report demonstrating that TRIM28 serves as a co-activator for ZFP30-mediated adipogenesis, and together these studies begin to establish that tripartite motif proteins may be bi-functional with respect to transcriptional repression or activation (Chen et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Discussion section based on the current findings and previous work.

claim: TRIM27 is a well characterized E3 ligase.
source: Notably, TRIM27 is also a well characterized E3 ligase and has been reported to modify numerous protein substrates via ubiquitination and SUMOylation (Chu and Yang, 2011; Zurek et al., 2012; Lee et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citations.

claim: TRIM27 has been reported to modify numerous protein substrates via ubiquitination and SUMOylation.
source: Notably, TRIM27 is also a well characterized E3 ligase and has been reported to modify numerous protein substrates via ubiquitination and SUMOylation (Chu and Yang, 2011; Zurek et al., 2012; Lee et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citations.

claim: Small molecule inhibitors of TRIM27 could selectively disrupt pro-tumorigenic TGFβ signaling in TNBC.
source: Future studies to address whether the catalytic activity of TRIM27 is required for ZNF165-dependent transcriptional regulation are therefore crucial, as small molecule inhibitors of TRIM27 could selectively disrupt pro-tumorigenic TGFβ signaling in TNBC.
evidence: This is a speculation stated in the Discussion section.

claim: RRAD is a TGFβ target gene that can exert opposing behaviors depending on context.
source: An additional, unexpected finding is that RRAD, whose transcription is highly regulated by the ZNF165 transcriptional complex, is a TGFβ target gene that can exert opposing behaviors depending on context.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Discussion section based on the experimental findings.

claim: TGFβ signaling drives pro-tumorigenic phenotypes in less differentiated breast tumor cell types, such as TNBC, while facilitating tumor suppression in more differentiated cell types.
source: TGFβ signaling is well known to drive pro-tumorigenic phenotypes in less differentiated breast tumor cell types, such as TNBC, while facilitating tumor suppression in more differentiated cell types (Tian et al., 2003; Massagué, 2008).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citations.

claim: RRAD contributes to context-specific phenotypes conferred by TGFβ signaling.
source: Our study indicates that RRAD contributes to such context-specific phenotypes conferred by TGFβ signaling, which may help to explain extensive data that report opposing impacts of RRAD expression in a variety of cancer types (Suzuki et al., 2007; Lee et al., 2010; Mo et al., 2012; Yeom et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Discussion section based on the experimental findings.

claim: RRAD is a small GTPase reported to negatively regulate L-type calcium channels in the heart.
source: With respect to function, RRAD is a small GTPase reported to negatively regulate L-type calcium channels in the heart, where its deficiency can promote cardiac hypertrophy (Chang et al., 2007; Manning et al., 2013; Meza et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citations.

claim: RRAD deficiency can promote cardiac hypertrophy.
source: With respect to function, RRAD is a small GTPase reported to negatively regulate L-type calcium channels in the heart, where its deficiency can promote cardiac hypertrophy (Chang et al., 2007; Manning et al., 2013; Meza et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citations.

claim: In cancer, RRAD has been implicated in the regulation of glycolysis, proliferation, NF-κB signaling, and apoptosis.
source: In cancer, RRAD has been implicated in numerous processes, including the regulation of glycolysis, proliferation, NF-κB signaling, and apoptosis (Lee et al., 2010; Yeom et al., 2012; Hsiao et al., 2014; Zhang et al., 2014; Liu et al., 2015; Shang et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citations.

claim: RRAD itself may be a tractable intervention point in TNBC.
source: Ultimately, further investigation could indicate that RRAD itself is a tractable intervention point in TNBC.
evidence: This is a speculation stated in the Discussion section.

claim: ZNF165 co-occupies a subset of SMAD3 genomic binding sites.
source: We find that ZNF165 co-occupies a subset of SMAD3 genomic binding sites and physically interacts with SMAD3 on chromatin, enhancing SMAD3 recruitment to specific loci.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the Introduction section.

claim: ZNF165 physically interacts with SMAD3 on chromatin.
source: We find that ZNF165 co-occupies a subset of SMAD3 genomic binding sites and physically interacts with SMAD3 on chromatin, enhancing SMAD3 recruitment to specific loci.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the Introduction section.

claim: ZNF165 enhances SMAD3 recruitment to specific loci.
source: We find that ZNF165 co-occupies a subset of SMAD3 genomic binding sites and physically interacts with SMAD3 on chromatin, enhancing SMAD3 recruitment to specific loci.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the Introduction section.

claim: Loss of function of the ZNF165-SMAD3 complex, through genetic inhibition of TRIM27, attenuates growth of an orthotopic xenograft model of TNBC in vivo.
source: Importantly, loss of function of this complex, through genetic inhibition of TRIM27, attenuates growth of an orthotopic xenograft model of TNBC in vivo.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the Introduction section.

claim: Anomalous expression of ZNF165 promotes the assembly of a neomorphic transcriptional complex that contributes to oncogenic TGFβ transcription in TNBC.
source: These findings establish that anomalous expression of ZNF165 promotes the assembly of a neomorphic transcriptional complex that contributes to oncogenic TGFβ transcription in TNBC.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion stated in the Introduction section.
